title: Rise, Rama
hookLine: the sage Vishvamitra wakes the boy Rama at dawn by the Sarayu: Hindus keep the day's joints, its twilights, with prayer
carry: hindus keep the day's joints with prayer
tomorrow: why did Rama wait out the rains?

cards: Still dark, on the bank of the Sarayu river. Two boys, the princes Rama and Lakshmana, are asleep on beds of grass. They've left the palace with the sage Vishvamitra, to guard his rituals from demons.
Before sunrise, the sage bends over them and wakes them, with words Hindus have sung ever since.

teach.b: In Valmiki's telling, Vishvamitra says: Rama, Kausalya's fine son, the eastern twilight is coming on. Rise, tiger among men; the day's rites to the gods are waiting. Kausalya supraja Rama, purva sandhya pravartate.

Those words open the Venkatesha Suprabhatam, the dawn hymn sung at Tirupati and played in countless homes before sunrise. The boys get up, bathe, and say their morning prayers by the river before walking on.
Sandhya means a joining: the twilight where night meets day, and day meets night. Here's the teaching. Hindus treat the joints of the day as sacred.

teach.h: A LAMP AT DUSK, QUIET TWILIGHTS
teach.b: The old practice is sandhyavandana, honoring the twilights with prayer, at dawn and dusk and for some at noon, with the Gayatri mantra at its heart.
Many families who don't keep the full rite still light a lamp at dusk, or play a suprabhatam at dawn.
Ayurveda notices the joints too: among its rules of good conduct, the Charaka Samhita advises against eating, sleeping or studying at the twilights, so they stay quiet.
And notice where the princes prayed: not in a palace, but on a riverbank, on the road. The practice traveled with them.
Today, that's the answer for a life that doesn't fit dawn to dusk: night shifts, a newborn, a job that starts at four.

teach.h: THE JOINTS MOVE WITH YOUR LIFE
teach.b: The joints don't disappear; they move. Waking, the first meal, the end of a shift. Hindus mark them wherever they are, the way two boys did by the Sarayu.

how: Some Hindus keep sandhyavandana, prayer with the Gayatri mantra at dawn and dusk (and for some at noon); many families light a lamp at dusk or play a dawn hymn such as the Venkatesha Suprabhatam before sunrise, and Ayurvedic texts advise keeping the twilights free of meals, sleep and study.

the day's conduct, which bends to fit the life keeping it
a fixed timetable that must be kept from dawn to dusk

games.q: the day's joints — tap the pairs.

s: the Venkatesha Suprabhatam opens with Vishvamitra's words to Rama
kausalya supraja rama, purva sandhya pravartate: the eastern twilight is coming on.
it's a joining, a twilight: where night meets day and day meets night.
Hindu twilight prayer only counts in a temple
Rama and Lakshmana prayed on a riverbank, on the road; the practice travels.

games.q: you work nights. the classical day starts before sunrise. what's the Hindu answer?
o: give it up: it isn't for you.
mark the joints your day really has, with a prayer or a breath.
games.why: the princes kept their dawn prayers on the road, by a river. the joints move with your life, and Hindus mark them where they are.

practice: Walk through a usual day, yours, not an ideal one, and find where one part bends into the next: waking, leaving the house, a meal, coming home, the last light switched off.

Choose one of those joints and see yourself pausing there for a single breath. If you pray, the Gayatri mantra or a prayer you already know can mark it; you can say a quiet Om now, as the breath goes out.

wordCard.voice: The daily routine. Dinacharya, from waking to twilight, with its sandhyas, the day's joints, kept with prayer.

orig.note: Sanskrit sandhya: a joining, a twilight; the junctions of the day marked by prayer in Hindu practice.

carryVoice: Your line: Hindus keep the day's joints with prayer. Two princes did it by a river. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 23.1–2 (Vishvamitra wakes Rama and Lakshmana by the Sarayu: 'kausalya supraja rama purva sandhya pravartate'; the princes bathe and do their morning rites)
Venkatesha Suprabhatam, verse 1 (opens with the same verse)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 8 (rules of good conduct, including not eating, sleeping or studying at the twilights)
